spoken: Imagine we fire tiny particles, one at a time, at a wall with two narrow slits in it.
And each one that gets through lands on the screen behind as a single dot.
At first, the dots seem to land almost anywhere.
Just random, then?
Keep going, though, and they sort themselves into stripes.
Stripes like these are what waves make when they overlap.
But we sent particles.
So what actually went through the slits? Was it a particle, or a wave?
That's the puzzle at the centre of the double-slit experiment.
People argued for centuries about what light actually is.
In his Treatise on Light, of sixteen ninety, Christiaan Huygens described light as a wave.
And Isaac Newton's Opticks, from 1704, leaned toward particles.
In later editions he asked, are not the rays of light very small bodies, emitted from shining substances?
So tiny bodies fly out of anything that shines.
And Newton's reputation was so great that, through the eighteenth century, the particle view held a wide lead.
So how would you even tell a wave from a stream of particles?
Send particles through two slits, and you'd expect two bright bands, one behind each slit.
But waves can do something particles can't. When two meet, they can add up, or cancel out.
Cancel out? Two waves can add up to nothing?
Crest on crest makes a bigger wave; crest on trough makes nothing at all. That's interference.
And particles, as far as anyone could see, shouldn't be able to do that.
Enter Thomas Young, a British doctor and polymath, who later helped decipher the Rosetta Stone.
From light waves to the Rosetta Stone, that's quite a range.
On the 24th of November, 1803, he described an experiment anyone could repeat, whenever the sun shines.
He let sunlight in through a small hole, and held a card a thirtieth of an inch wide in the beam.
In the card's shadow appeared coloured fringes, which were stripes of light and dark.
That's in the shadow, where you'd expect plain darkness.
And when he blocked the light on one side of the card, the fringes vanished.
So the fringes needed light from both sides, meeting and interfering.
So it's really a two-path experiment, just with a card instead of slits.
And his lectures, published in eighteen oh seven, describe the version we know, with light through two narrow slits.
Though whether he ever actually did it with two slits isn't clear.
So the famous version may have been partly a thought experiment.
Either way, the turn came in 1818, when Augustin Fray-nel entered a French prize contest with a wave theory.
One judge, Simeon Pwasson, spotted what looked like an absurd prediction.
What was it?
In the middle of a small round disc's shadow, the theory said, there should be a bright spot.
So the head of the judges, Fran-swah Arago, tried it, and there was the spot.
The absurd prediction came true.
After that, most scientists accepted that light is a wave.
And in eighteen sixty-five, James Clark Maxwell predicted it's an electromagnetic wave, so the particle idea seemed finished.
Seemed.
So how do two slits make a whole row of stripes, not just two bands?
Each slit acts as a new source, sending out waves that spread in circles.
And to reach a point on the screen, one wave usually travels a little farther than the other.
If that extra distance is a whole number of wavelengths, crests arrive together, and the spot is bright.
And if it's half a wavelength, crest meets trough, and the spot is dark.
Slide along the screen and the extra distance grows steadily, so the stripes go bright, dark, bright, dark.
So the spacing of the stripes should follow from the geometry.
It does. It's the wavelength, times the distance to the screen, divided by the gap between the slits.
Take slits half a millimetre apart, light with a wavelength of zero point six micrometres, and a screen one metre away.
Then the stripes come out one point two millimetres apart.
Move the screen twice as far away, and they spread twice as wide.
And if the slits move closer together?
They spread out too. Young described stripes wider also in the same proportion as the apertures are closer to each other.
And it works backwards too. Young used fringes like these to estimate the wavelengths of colours, close to modern values.
So he measured a wave far too small to see, just from the stripes.
But the wave picture had a crack in it.
In 1905, Albert Einstein proposed that light's energy comes in separate lumps, now called photons.
Lumps of light? After Young and Maxwell?
It explained the photoelectric effect, and later won him a Nobel Prize.
That raises a question. What happens to the stripes when light is so dim that it arrives a little at a time?
In 1909, a young Cambridge physicist, Geoffrey Ingram Taylor, tried it.
He dimmed a gas light with dark glass, until it was like a candle more than a mile away.
A candle more than a mile off? That's faint.
It was so faint that his photographic plate, behind a sewing needle, took three months to expose.
And the fringes were still there.
As Paul Dirac later put it, each photon then interferes only with itself.
Interferes with itself. That's a strange sentence.
It is. And one caution is that Taylor's paper never mentions photons, and his dim lamp wasn't a true single-photon source.
So it was very faint light, not strictly one photon at a time.
The real test came in nineteen eighty-six, when a French team including Alain Aspect used a genuine single-photon source and an interferometer.
And the interference was still there, one photon at a time.
Here, each photon is detected at one single point.
A few hundred look like noise.
But by ten thousand, the stripes are unmistakable.
And with brighter light?
The dots just pile up faster, giving the same pattern, sooner.
Electrons came the other way round. From eighteen ninety-seven, experiments showed them behaving as particles.
Then, in 1924, Louis de Broy proposed that all matter has a wave side too.
All matter? Electrons, atoms, everything?
In principle, yes.
And in nineteen twenty-seven, experiments confirmed it for electrons, bouncing them off crystals and through thin films.
But for decades, the two-slit version with electrons was taught only as a thought experiment.
This experiment, Richard Feynman even wrote in his famous lectures, has never been done in just this way.
Except it had, in 1961, the year those lectures began.
So who did it?
Klaus Yernsson, in Tubingen, made slits for electrons and saw the fringes, with up to five slits.
His paper was in German, and didn't appear in English until nineteen seventy-four.
That same year, in Bologna, Merli, Missiroli and Pozzi sent electrons through one at a time.
They didn't use slits, though. They used an electron biprism, which is a fine wire that splits the beam in two.
Then in 1989, Akira Tonomura and colleagues at Hitachi made it cleaner still.
Fewer than a thousand electrons arrived each second, so two were never in the apparatus at once.
So there was nothing for an electron to interfere with, except itself.
Each one arrived as a single flash. Here are eight electrons, then two hundred and seventy, then two thousand.
And over a twenty-minute exposure, 60,000 electrons drew the stripes.
In two thousand and two, Physics World readers voted the single-electron version the most beautiful experiment in physics.
So how big can a thing be and still do this?
In nineteen ninety-one, helium atoms interfered after passing through slits in gold foil.
In 1999, a team in Vienna sent buckyballs, molecules of 60 carbon atoms, through a grating of many slits.
A buckyball is zero point seven nanometres across, and its wave was some two hundred and eighty times smaller.
A wave far smaller than the molecule, and it still interfered?
It did.
And the record kept growing, to molecules of 810 atoms in 2013, and about 2,000 atoms in 2019.
Then in twenty twenty-six, a team in Vienna showed interference with sodium clusters, some of more than seven thousand atoms.
That's seven thousand atoms, behaving like a wave.
The heavier the object, the shorter its wave, and the harder its stripes are to see.
So is there a size where it simply stops?
That's still debated, but so far quantum theory has passed every one of these tests.
Now comes the most famous twist.
Put a detector at each slit, to find out which one each particle goes through.
Every particle is found at one slit or the other, never split between them.
And the stripes vanish.
They're gone, just from checking the path.
The screen now shows two single-slit patterns, simply added together, with no interference.
Why? To learn the path, the detector has to interact with the particle.
And that leaves a record of which way it went, so the two paths can no longer interfere.
And that's where the popular story goes wrong.
It's often told as if a conscious observer changes the outcome, but the standard account needs no mind at all.
So no one has to be watching?
No. What matters is whether the path could be known, in principle, from anything left behind.
In 2004, for example, a Vienna team laser-heated carbon-70 molecules, so they gave off heat radiation in flight.
That radiation carried traces of each molecule's path, and the hotter the molecules, the fainter the stripes.
And nobody looked at that light; it only had to exist.
The molecules gave themselves away.
And it isn't all or nothing. A 1987 experiment gathered some path information and kept fainter stripes.
The better the two paths can be told apart, the fainter the stripes have to be.
So it's a trade-off, not an on-off switch.
Richard Feynman put this experiment at the centre of quantum physics.
He called it impossible, absolutely impossible, to explain in any classical way.
It has in it the heart of quantum mechanics, he said. In reality, it contains the only mystery.
The only mystery? Those are strong words.
So in quantum mechanics, each particle is described by a wave that passes through both slits.
The wave only sets the odds of where each particle lands, and those odds are the square of the wave at each spot.
Each detection is still a single dot, and only the pile of dots reveals the wave.
But what is it doing between the slits and the screen?
That's exactly where interpretations of quantum mechanics part ways.
In one view, asking which slit means nothing without a detector; in others, there are many worlds, or a guiding wave.
But they all predict the same stripes, dot for dot.
So Young's stripes showed light is a wave, and single dots showed it arrives in lumps.
Then electrons, atoms and molecules turned out to do exactly the same.
And a record of the path, of any kind, wipes the stripes away.
And it all comes from a wall with two slits in it.
With two slits, a screen, and one dot at a time, it's still the clearest view we have of the quantum world.
